Washington, June 25.—War Department officials announced unofficially yesterday that the exemption regulations by which thousands of men expect to escape military service under the Selective Draft Act will be so rigid as to excuse but few in addition to detectives.

War service of an active character either abroad or at home is to be provided for all within the age limit. The official publication of the regulations is expected within the next 48 hours.

Men engaged in pursuits necessary to the prosecution of the war are to be classified and organized into a separate army. As rapidly as their places can be filled by men able to do the same work but physically unfit for the battlefields, they will be sent to join an active military command.

Men who claim wholly dependent families will be investigated. They will be excused if the claim is found to be just, but not dropped from the roster. This class will be used to organize a home guard defense where the necessity arises.

It was said the actual process of drafting the National army will begin around July 10. It is hoped to begin the work before that date, but the magnitude of the task has caused the War Department machinery to slow down.

The interference of politicians who wished to exercise influence in the appointment of local exemption boards has been another cause of delay. Governors in many states who hold this power were not able to act until the regulations published last week were actually in their hands. Where it is possible state machinery is to be used, but in many states entirely new boards are being created.

Sonora. were arrested here today in connection with an alleged shortage of $60,000 in the accounts of the Mexican custom house at that point and are held in jail here for possible extradition to Sonora. The arrest of the two men resulted from a dispute between them and the driver of an automobile which brought them here from Nogales. When the men were arrested they told the officers of the discovery by Mexican officials of the deficit in the custom house funds and said they had fled for fear they would be executed on suspicion that they were involved in the shortage.

 According to the driver of the auto mobile, a third man left Nogales by another route. carrying with him part of the $60000 alleged to have been stolen from the custom house funds.

EL PASO, Texas, Febrero 15.
Francisco Villa ha tenido hasta ahora establecido su Cuartel general establecido en el rancho de Bustillos, propiedad de Alberto Mauero, donde varios miles de hombres estaban reconcentrados, bajo su personal comando. El jefe, de quien muy pocas o ningunas noticias ciertas se tenían, ha instalado un sistema telegráfico que comunica su Cuartel general con la zona del Noroeste con lo que ha estado al tanto de los movimientos de las fuerzas carrancistas, pues se comunica diariamente con los diferentes jefes villistas que ha enviado a operar a diversos puntos, hasta la frontera con los Estados Unidos.

All entertaining for this week will center about THANKSGIVING Day, and a great many dinner parties have been planned at the clubs and in private homes, not only for guests from distance, but FOR the men from Camp Lee. The football game Thursday between Washington and Lee and Washington and Jefferson Universities will be a big society event, and the Colors of the two colleges will be used everywhere with the flags of the nation as decorations for the functions given to honor the two teams. Buffet luncheons will be given before the game, and one of the most interesting of these will be that at which Mrs. H. L. Ellington, of Monument Avenue, will be HOSTESS. The luncheon will be given for some of the visiting college boys, and will be a very smart affair.

Two interesting entertainments of note will take place THANKSGIVING night. Miss Ella Binford has charge of the usual THANKSGIVING german, which is to be held in the ballroom of the Jefferson Hotel from 9 to 1, and is given by the girls of Richmond in honor of the visiting football teams. A portion of the proceeds will be a gift to the Red Cross, and a brilliant company of guests will attend it. The ball will be opened with a figure led by Miss Virginia Ellington and Braxton Valentine, those taking part to include the young girls who were to have made their debut in Richmond this winter. These are Misses Margaret Powers, Margaret Herndon, Mildred Williams, Catherine Valentine, Ellen Wallace, Rose Caperton, Catherine Peasants, Carrie Taliaferro, Hazeltine Watson, Marie Wilkinson, Muria Adkins, Lewis Warren, Antoinette Hermann and Laura Nelson.

The concert and vaudeville to be given at the City Auditorium at 8 o'clock the same evening to equip the band of the 315th Regiment will be another attractive event, and hundreds of prominent guests will be present. Many parties will attend the concert early in the evening, going later to attend the ball at the Jefferson.

The marriage of Miss Imogen Riddick, daughter of Mr. and Mrs. Junius Roane Riddick, to Robert Tucker Hunter will be celebrated very quietly Tuesday evening, at 7 o'clock at 40 Allen Avenue, the home of Mr. and Mrs. Charles A. Page. Only the immediate families will be present.

Wednesday evening Miss Frances X. Scott is giving an informal dance at her home, 11 West Franklin Street, in honor of her niece, Miss Isabel Scott, Miss Mary Wingfield Scott and Miss Mary Austen Campden; only the younger society set and some of the officers have been included in the invitations.

More entertainment has been planned for THANKSGIVING week than at any time since the fall season began and there will be many visitors in Richmond for the holiday.

The marriage of Miss Jessie Lillian Thomas, daughter of Mr. and Mrs. John Daniel Thomas, of Louisa, to Lieutenant Fred Gore Rockwell, of the Three Hundred and Fifth Engineers, United States Army, will take place on Monday afternoon, December 5, at 3 o'clock, in the Church of the Incarnation at Mineral. Lieutenant Rockwell is stationed at Camp Lee.

A reception for Mrs. Flournoy, Lee Chapter United Daughters of the Confederacy, will be given Tuesday afternoon from 3 to 5 o'clock at the Confederate Woman's Home in honor of Mrs. Cabell Flournoy, the newly elected president, of the Richmond.

demand for everything will, no doubt,
grow greater in this country during

"When I was in Georgia there was plenty of bourbon and very little quinine. Now YOU can get all the quinine YOU want, but very little liquor. It's tough on people who are liable TO get fever and ague. I'll see if I can get some medicine for YOU from some of these Confederate veterans. I don't think they would refuse attention to an honorable foe like Private Jerry Donovan."

The Private Corrects His Son

Whether or not Shocker submitted to the treatment prescribed by Private Donovan, his case was pronounced greatly improved by evening; probably the quinine did it.

The ball players, made languid by this air, which IS particularly and peculiarly adapted for dreaming away the days in restful indolence, began TO pray for shower. Anybody who has read anything about the war appreciates the rigor as well as the danger and daring of the aviation service. Those who shivered at the touch of frost can scarcely imagine the chill of the upper air, but no matter how cold it is the flyer must not only keep going but fighting at the same time, for it is always his life or that of his foe, with no escape for one of the two. After such ride and race with death the physical craving for stimulant is acute. The most welcome refreshment to the aviator is a bit of sugar, and it is this morsel which is so scarce and so difficult to obtain in France. This aviator begged for a taste of it.

Sugar is one of the foods which the people have been asked to conserve so that more can be sent abroad to relieve the famine there among both soldiers and civilians. It was told very lately how Washington, the national capital, was without sugar for days because of the car shortage. Three carloads from Louisiana took months to get there despite special attention. Add on the difficulties and delays of shipping, and it can be seen how hard it is to land sugar from this country in France. Yet the sugar must all come from this country, the war stopping manufacture abroad.

The American people are loyal to their country and devoted to their soldiers and to the allies fighting for them. They would not knowingly consent to sending their boys thousands of miles to face and fight ruthless enemy, and then stab their defenders in the back by taking the food away from the boys. Teaching the children the reasons for conservation will spread the knowledge to the homes. The churches, organized womanhood, and other agencies are performing systematic service. The following-up of a pledge card campaign is vital and will be an effective work. The Food Administration is supplying supplementary kitchen cards and other literature to drive the conservation doctrine deeper home. Every home must be enlisted. Every hotel and restaurant must also serve meatless and wheatless days. Everybody must be encouraged and induced to save the few foods which can easiest be shipped and which can be kept longest without spoiling. The sacrifice which the American people are asked to make in the way of food saving is infinitesimal in comparison. A bit of sugar is a very small reward for an aviator returning from battle in the distant skies, in which every nerve was strained to the breaking point. It was that bit of sugar which his own people denied him, though they thought they were proving their patriotism in many ways. It is that bit of sugar which the Food Administration is trying to teach the people to give gladly, especially as it will not deprive them in any way.

A program at Bowersock's theater included addresses by prominent men of the state. Among the speakers at the theater were C. S. Gleed of Topeka, one of the directors of the Santa Fe; former Governor George H. Hodges; J. L. Bristow, chairman of the state public utilities commission; H. G. Kali, general Union Pacific at Kansas City; J. J. Helm, president of the Kansas City, Kaw Valley & Western Interurban company; J. S. Amick, county attorney of Douglas county; Thomas Harley, city attorney of Lawrence; Benjamin T. Wilson, Williamstown; George Innes, Lawrence; A. A. Andrews, Baldwin, and others. H. C. Pribble of Topeka, claim agent for the Santa Fe, was one of the men prominent in the celebration.

The new bridge replaces an ancient and dilapidated structure which has done duty for many years. It is of the county. Many railroad men are participating in the program on account of the fact that thru taxation they have contributed a large share of the money which built the bridge. An extensive approach across the Santa Fe tracks was necessary.

The celebration included a procession across the bridge, the meeting at the theater and other features. Cafes in Lawrence served dinner free to the guests, and the theaters gave free performances during the afternoon.

The Kansas City, Kaw Valley & Western Interurban line, which at present reaches Lawrence from Kansas City will use the bridge.

A sighting remark passed in a conversation regarding the fire which destroyed the 450-foot wharf at the immigration station below Algiers. Tuesday afternoon, led to the arrest of Fred Paulsen, a Norwegian sailor. I could easily have put the fire out, said Paulsen to the crew of a streetcar that carried him from the immigration station to the Canal street ferry.

Motorman Lacoste and Conductor Mares became suspicious when Paulsen boarded the car. He wanted to know if it would leave immediately. After that, he made the remark quietly. When they asked why he did not help extinguish the fire Paulsen said he did not consider it any of his business.

They told J. Z. Salvant, assistant superintendent of the road and Corporal Jack Carlin, of the Marines at the immigration station. Paulsen was turned over to Police Corporal A. C. Prados. Sergeant William Peterson began an investigation and Paulsen was held for the Federal Court.

The fire was discovered at 1:00 o'clock at a distant part of the wharf which stood about 100 feet off shore from Mayo, immigration commissioner. He summoned all the employees of the station, but the men made little progress. The property was destroyed when firemen reached the scene owing to the delay in sending in an alarm. The loss is $4,000.

Commissioner Mayo expressed the belief that the flames were due to sparks from a passing vessel. He said the wharf was guarded by Marines and no one was allowed on it.

hanging arms, crushed by the heavi-

stopped to think, we would know that
the spiritual things make life; that
without love and JOY and unselfishness
and courage we could not long endure
the daily mortal round of dressing and
eating and sleeping. If there is any
such thing as eternal life, this present
life is part of it, and why not go light

plodding through them? We may, if

life and crush out all spiritual eager-

G. Demers, 81, was drowned in Black

noon Sunday, when he fell from a ledge

slipped in the mud and fell headlong in
to the waters of the Black River. Mr.

Company of this town, and had been
in poor health for some time. He leaves
a wife and six children, the oldest of
whom is only ten years of age. A

WASHINGTON, March 5.--The entire National Guard of the United States will be called to the colors probably within 48 hours from the time President Wilson approves the declaration of war against Germany.

About the same time the naval militia of the country will be ordered to mobilize, and all the services of both services not now under arms, will be summoned to duty.

President Has Power.

THESE steps may be taken without further legislation by Congress or any further grant of power to the President. All that he is now waiting for is the passage of the resolution which gives this country definite belligerent status.

Other steps for this creation of additional military forces will be considered by Congress while the Guard and the naval militia are reporting for duty. As soon as acted upon the war program of the administration in this direction will be put into effect with all possible dispatch.

As soon as the state troops are mobilized and mustered in, wherein a campaign will be launched to recruit these organizations to full war strength. This campaign will be along much the same lines as now followed by the navy and the marine corps.

Plans Formed Long Ago.

It was learned, moreover, that the administration has had in view from the beginning the complete mobilization of the National Guard and that the only reason why all of the troops were not called at once—after war was seen to be inevitable—was that the War Department did not want to muster in state organizations faster than the regular army officers could equip them.

Much experience was gained in this direction when the Guard was called to the colors for service on the Mexican border. The War Department was literally overwhelmed by its task of providing food, clothing, camp outfits and other field equipment to 125,000 soldiers. There was no panic or even confusion in the distribution but the job was enormous and which had to be performed by troops.

In the light of this experience, the General Staff has advised the administration to call out the 2nd year groups and this policy has been followed with the result that the several commands now in the field have been equipped, inspected and mustered into the federal service with dispatch hitherto impossible.

Naval Militia Due Soon.

The naval militia may expect to get an order to mobilize about the same time the National Guard is called out. Secretary Daniels and Secretary Baker have conferred upon those questions and it is stated that they are prepared to issue the mobilization order to each branch of the reserve just as soon as the war resolution is passed and signed.

Details of the recruiting campaign, designed to bring the National Guard up to war strength, have not been discussed, except in general terms, but the understanding is that this campaign will be carried on with great vigor and the result will be used as an indication of the willingness of American men to volunteer for service in the war. If few men offer themselves for this service, the fact largely will guide the administration in its plan of creating additional forces.

WASHINGTON. March 26.—Organization of the new house by Democrats was declared to be assured tonight by Representative Randall of California, prohibitionist, and one of the five so called independents upon whom the political complexion of the house has seemed to hinge.

Mr. Randall returned to Washington tonight from Los Angeles. On reading a statement issued during the day by Republican Leader Mann offering to retire from the race for speakership in favor of Speaker Clark if a bipartisan or nonpartisan organization were agreed, he said Mr. Mann was too late, that he was in position to say that enough of the Independents would vote with the Democrats to give the latter a majority and assure the administration of control by its party of both houses of Congress.

While the entente may combine their resources and in time secure a popular victory, yet they all must come from warfare crippled and impoverished. SANTA FE, N. M. Sept. 6—Evidence of a pre-Pueblo culture thousands of years old have been discovered by Dr. Byron Cummings of the University of Arizona, and Prof. Frederick W. Hodge of the Bureau of American Ethnology, in excavations just completed in Arizona and New Mexico.

On Navajo mountain, on the Navajo reservation near the New Mexico Arizona boundary, Dr. Cummings broke into Antelope clans of the Hopi and secured many priceless relics.

Within the week three guardsmen of the regiment have died of pneumonia. The sickness is attributed to the change in climate they experienced when they were brought to Idaho from the Mexican border. Officers say the men were careless with their clothing and colds and sickness followed.

Those who have died are Capt. L. Shaw of Payette, who had been ill for months; Sergeant Cupit of the Ceur d'Alene company; Privates "Ted" Sullivan of Portland and Barlow of Weiser.

Sickness and alleged insanitary conditions at the barracks led to a clash in the legislature. An investigation was demanded by Nelson, Daughters, Kiger and others, which was opposed by Moody, who intimated the complaints were exaggerated.

When forged signature is suspected the method adopted is to take photographs of the genuine and supposed false signatures, magnify each hundredfold or more and compare the results. Under this careful test the slightest discrepancy becomes exaggerated out of close resemblance to the signature, and every sign of hesitancy—for few forgers can write counterfeit signature with perfect ease and fluency—stands revealed.
A forged banknote, however minutely and faithfully the original may have been copied, cannot deceive the eye of the camera, which will show not only the slightest deviation from the genuine note, but also any difference in the texture of the paper used. In a recent case, where a section of a check had been removed and another piece in the form of pulp substituted with unusual skill, the camera revealed the fraud at once, showing exactly where the new and old papers were joined.

Sir: The bill for health insurance introduced by Senator Ogden L. Mills embodies the principle that the financial expense of illness in workmen's families can be more certainly and more satisfactorily met by insurance than by savings. It has been reported to The News through various channels that the farmers of the different areas around Springdale have taken exceptions to the campaign of Prepare Feed Yourself, which has just closed.

These exceptions, objections, seem to come from farmers who state that they do not need any information from Springdale citizens, business men or anyone else as to how to farm. It is to be sincerely regretted that such feeling exists in the mind of even the most insignificant farmer in this section. The farmer who takes this view of the recent campaign is insignificant and would be the first to ask aid of the people of Springdale in his family and stock without food. For this class of farmers, if there be such in this section, and doubt it seriously, we have sympathy. They do belong to that class of Americans who themselves are not farmers; they belong to that class that should not claim the protection of American made laws, but should be relegated to a secluded spot of earth, and make for themselves a home. We have sympathy for farmers who above such accusations.

The different speakers who went out from Springdale did not make any pretense of telling farmers how to farm. That was not their mission. They are true blue Americans and took the opportunity offered to do patriotic work and they responded; they are doing their bit. Their mission was to take to the farmers a message direct from President Wilson to the people of the South, and of Arkansas. That message was for the farmers of Arkansas to "prepare to feed themselves." It was a message urging the farmers to "do their bit" by planting and cultivating crops to conserve the crop they did raise and a message bringing to the farmers the present food and feed situation so that they might understand. It was a message telling of the crisis in feed and food in the United States; it was a message urging Arkansas farmers to make every effort to stop the importing of $65,000,000 worth of feed and food stuff into the state in a single year.

There was nothing in the message to tell farmers how to farm. The speakers who went from Springdale carried such a message. Perhaps the speakers brought out the points of better farming, intensive farming and others, but they did not make any attempt to tell farmers how to farm. The speakers who went out from Springdale were only a few of the many that came from different states throughout the Southland. They gave of their time and energy, and gave freely; no financial consideration was thought of—it was a patriotic mission, much the same as the young man who shoulders a gun and fights for his country. They were the first line of defense of a movement that will surely devastate this section unless the message they carried is received in the proper manner—and the farmers go to work.

All hail to the speakers who carried the message, and all hail to the farmers who received it in the proper spirit, and are this moment falling in line to feed themselves and help feed the boys in the trenches.

Today is the fortieth anniversary OF
Bismarck'S first great fire, which
practically destroyed the 5-year-old
citys business district.


At 8 o'clock in the morning, Satur-
day, March II, 1877, someone who had
started early celebrating St. Patrick's
day kicked over the stove in the piO-
neer Main street saloon, known as
The Hole-in-the-Wall. The flames
spread quickly to adjoining frame and
log buildings, and before the blaze
could be controlled everything from
John Olstand's down TO and including
the Western house, or from the cor
ner of Fifth and Main, where the Nc
kenzie now stands, to the present site
Of RichmOnd's shoe store, was Destroy
ed.


Pioneers Lost Heavily.


Among those who suffered in the
conhagration was j. p. Dunn, whose
drug store burned to the ground; Asa
Fisher, owner Of large two-story log
building at the corner of Main and
Fifth, occupied by saloon; John P.
Yegen, Bismarck's pioneer baker, and
Thomas MCGOWAN, all Of whom lost
practically everything they had in the
way of buildings and contents.


Made Yegen Dutchman.


John Yegen was one Of the heaviest
losers. The Tribune the week fol-
lowing the fire says Of him: John
Yegen, when asked as to the extent
of his loss. said, when he went to
bed the night before he was an Am
erican citizen, but now he is a Dutch
man again, as his naturalization pa
pers were burned, and that, he guess
ed. was his greatest loss. The re-
mains of nearly a thousand dollars
were still smoking, and he had not
yet learned that about 40 barrels OF
apples and other supplies in the Gel
lar were safe. Next day Yegen show
ed his customers all lie saved from
the fire, as he called it, in the shape
of a ledger showing the amount due
from the curious inspector, who in al
most every instance went to the bot
tom of his pocket to help Johnny, as
everyone calls him, rebuild


Rebuilt at Once.


With characteristic bismarck cOur-
age and enterprise, the task of re-
building was begun at once. J. P.
Dunn purchased the cid Congregation
al church, standing where the court
house now is located, and moved it to
his Main street lot; John Yegen re-

the semi-finals of the Pan-Hellenic
Baseball League yesterday afternoon.
This makes Phi Delta Theta the cham
pion of its division and leaves only
one game between Phi Delta Theta
and Phi Gamma Delta to decide the
championship.


The cup which goes each year to
the winner of the series is now in the
possession of the Sigma Nu fraternity,
that organization having won last
years championship. In order to own
the cup one fraternity must hold it for
three successive years.


The Phi Delta Thetas will play the
Phi Cams at 3:44 tomorrow afternoon
on Rollins Field, to decide the league
championship.

WASHINGTON, March 6.—Machinery looking to the prompt execution of his program for speeding up naval construction was set in motion today by Secretary Daniels. He conferred with Representatives of the major shipbuilding companies and later with Secretary Wilson of the labor department and Samuel Gompers of the American Federation of Labor. President Wilson called at the navy department during the day and talked with Mr. Daniels for some time. The president was told that even with an emergency fund of more than $100,900, backed by authority to require preference for navy orders and if necessary to take over shipyards or other plans, it would be difficult to get ships rushed to completion.

The shipbuilders will present tomorrow detailed statements of what they might be able to do with additional funds in the way of speeding up. They will also show just what additional work each plant may be able to undertake.

The most serious problem is that of securing skilled labor, although suspension of the eight hour law on government contracts is expected to help in this regard. Mr. Daniels asked the advice of Secretary Wilson and Mr. Gompers as to what steps to take to increase the supply of labor in the ship trades.

A conference of steel makers and other concerns which supply material for the navy will be called shortly, to be followed by similar meetings with representatives of smaller shipbuilding companies which are not now engaged on government work.

The president, under the law, has power to require such companies to place their full facilities at the disposal of the government by issuing a proclamation declaring an emergency to exist.

Con l'arrivo dei rinforzi lo sforzo della guarnigione dei posti avanzati il nemico fu respinto e costretto a ritirarsi nelle posizioni dalle quali era partito. Altri reparti nemici tentarono simili azioni a Crodade, Longelini, Pabola-Visdende. Essi furono dispersi dal nostro efficace fuoco.

A sud di Tolmino le nostre batterie bombardarono con successo una colonna in movimento composta di numerosi autocarri.

Ieri ad incursione di gorilla alcuni nostri reparti, dopo violenta preparazione dell'artiglieria, eseguirono una incursione nelle caverne situate sulle pendici nordiche di Monte San Gabrielle e presero prigionieri un ufficiale e ventitré uomini di truppa.

Notizie dalla fronte belga recano che le truppe britanniche continuano a riportare notevoli successi nelle Fiandre, ove hanno respinto i tedeschi, che si sono dati alla fuga ed al quale hanno inflitto perdite enormi, una grande quantità di prigionieri e di materiale da guerra.

Il Governo di Pietrogrado annunzia pure importanti vittorie conseguite dalle truppe russe. Il comunicato ufficiale dice che esploratori russi dell'armata del Caucaso son riusciti a far prigioniero il generale Count Von Meyer, capo dei servizi aerei tedeschi nel distretto del Mar Nero.

Noble does not believe the primary law is greatly demanded by the voters. He is opposed to the measure, he stated, both because of the enormous expense attached to the operation of the law and inability of the measure to reform or improve the election system.

Travis, of Allen county declared he would offer a bill opposing the primary. Travis was made administration whip in an effort to grease the troubled legislative waters—and Travis forgot to offer his bill.

Mack's Many Reforms.
Representative C. C. Mack of Harvey county, today loaded the calendar with proposed reforms. He introduced a bill providing for state construction of hard surface roads and the establishment of a state highway commission. A two-mill road levy is provided by the bill for hard surface roads. The measure also permits the state to participate in use of the federal road fund.

Mack also offered a resolution providing for submission to the voters of a proposition for a constitutional convention. In an effort to avoid trouble in submission of a possible proposed constitution, Mack would submit amendments providing for submission of more than three amendments in a single election and for ratification of a call for a constitutional convention by a majority of the votes cast on the proposition.

The Minister of Denmark, Constan-
tin Brun, returned to Washington last
evening after passing the summer at
Bar Harbor.

general munitions board, who is out

house in Washington for the win-

Captain James at Fort Myer.

Captain and Mrs. Alexander Long
James, jr., who have been in the West
for some time, have come to Fort
Myer, Va., where they are to be sta-
tioned indefinitely. Captain James
was on duty at Fort Myer about three
years ago. He was married last Feb-
ruary to Miss Viola Burden, daughter
of Mr. and Mrs. George Albert Bur-
den, of Hollywood, Cal. Mrs. James
is handsome and clever, and will be
a charming addition to society this
winter.
